sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

"AI on-call teammate" became a real, mainstream product category in 2025-2026, not a research demo: Datadog Bits AI SRE, PagerDuty's AI Agent Suite (built around its SRE Agent), New Relic SRE Agent, AWS DevOps Agent, and incident.io's AI SRE all now investigate alerts, correlate telemetry, and propose (sometimes execute) fixes before a human engineer has even opened their laptop. This lesson tours that category honestly — including the real gap between vendors willing to auto-remediate and vendors who refuse on principle — and then covers a genuine, disclosed 2026 security incident, nicknamed "agentjacking," where attackers turned the exact kind of telemetry pipeline these agents read from into a way to hijack Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex sessions. You'll finish having audited one real trust boundary in a tool or integration you actually use, and written down where human accountability has to sit before you'd let any of these agents near production.

## What an AI SRE Agent Actually Does

The clearest example is **Datadog Bits AI SRE** (launched as "Bits Investigation" at DASH in December 2025, with a faster, deeper-reasoning update through 2026). It works completely autonomously once an alert fires — no prompting required. It analyzes runbooks and telemetry, forms a root-cause hypothesis, validates its own findings, and can deliver a conclusion to Slack or Microsoft Teams before an on-call engineer has even logged in. The 2026 update added MCP-powered tool integration and cut investigation time to roughly 3-4 minutes, with access to Real User Monitoring, Database Monitoring, and Network Path Analysis alongside the core telemetry. On the action side, Bits can execute defined triage steps automatically — creating an incident, paging the right engineer, opening a Jira ticket, prefilling it with the affected services and suspected root cause — and it has been tested against more than 2,000 customer environments.

This is the shape of the whole category: read broadly across an organization's observability data, form a hypothesis fast, and either hand a human a head start or take a bounded, defined action itself.

## The Spectrum: How Much Autonomy Each Vendor Actually Grants

The five major platforms differ less in what they can technically do and more in how much they're willing to act without a human in the loop:

- **PagerDuty's AI Agent Suite** is building toward a literal "virtual responder" that sits directly on a team's escalation policy — the only one of the five structured that way. Its SRE Agent handles autonomous detection, triage, and diagnosis before a human is paged, and it's rolling out in phases: virtual-responder early access in Q2 2026, a fully autonomous responder tier reaching early access only in H2 2026 — a deliberately staged rollout, not a single switch.
- **New Relic SRE Agent** is the conservative outlier by explicit design. Its stated philosophy is to "accelerate understanding, not take action on its own" — it refuses to auto-remediate on principle, reasoning that a false-positive automated restart that takes down a payment system costs far more than a false-negative page that simply wakes an engineer a few minutes later.
- **AWS DevOps Agent** publishes real case-study numbers rather than only projected ones: Western Governors University reported a mean-time-to-resolution drop from roughly 2 hours to 28 minutes, a 77% reduction, using AWS DevOps Agent integrated with PagerDuty. It still requires explicit human approval before taking action.
- **incident.io's AI SRE** claims to handle the first 80% of incident response — investigation and drafting — but its remediation feature, "Code it up," drafts a pull request rather than auto-merging it.

The common thread across every credible platform in this category: **remediation stays behind a human approval gate.** As one industry analysis of the space put it, until these tools can reliably distinguish "I'm 99% sure" from "I'm 70% sure" — and most currently cannot — a human gate on the action itself is standard practice, not a limitation vendors are racing to remove.

## The Agentjacking Incident: When the Telemetry Feed Itself Is the Attack

In June 2026, the AI-agent security firm Tenet Security disclosed an attack it calls **"agentjacking"** — and it's directly relevant to anyone running an AI SRE agent, or any coding agent, on top of an observability or error-tracking pipeline.

The mechanism: **Sentry**, the error-monitoring service wired into thousands of applications, accepts arbitrary error-event payloads from anyone who has a project's DSN (data source name) — by design, since that's how client applications report crashes. Separately, the Sentry MCP server returns that event data to AI coding agents as trusted system output. Tenet's researchers found they could craft a fake Sentry error event containing instructions visually and structurally indistinguishable from Sentry's own legitimate remediation guidance. When a developer asked their agent to "fix this Sentry error," agents including **Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex** interpreted the injected text as genuine diagnostic steps and executed attacker-controlled npm packages — no phishing, no server breach, just a crafted event sent to a public ingestion endpoint.

The scale Tenet reported: an **85% success rate** across the most popular agents, tested against over 100 real-world targets, and **at least 2,388 organizations** found to have valid, injectable Sentry DSNs exposed. It's worth being precise about what that figure does and doesn't mean, since the accurate version is already concerning enough without embellishment: 2,388 is the count of organizations whose Sentry configuration *could* be exploited this way, using only public Sentry APIs and breaching nothing — it is **not** a count of confirmed compromises. Exploitation still requires that organization to be running an agent connected to Sentry with command-execution privileges. Tenet did confirm successful agent execution at specific organizations spanning Fortune 100 companies down to individual developers, disclosed the flaw to Sentry on June 3, 2026, and Sentry called the underlying architectural issue "technically not defensible," adding a content filter for the specific proof-of-concept payload string. The Cloud Security Alliance classified agentjacking as a systemic MCP vulnerability class within days.

## Why This Slipped Past Every Traditional Defense

The detail that should genuinely concern anyone running these tools: **every step of an agentjacking attack is individually authorized.** The attacker never touches the victim's infrastructure. The developer never approves anything that looks like a malicious action — they approved "go read the Sentry error and fix it," which is exactly what the agent did. Tenet calls this the **Authorized Intent Chain**, and it's precisely why EDR, WAF, IAM controls, VPNs, and firewalls registered nothing worth flagging — none of those tools are positioned to evaluate whether the *content* an agent trusts is itself hostile. Even prompt-level defenses failed in testing: agents ran the injected payload even when system prompts and skills explicitly instructed them to ignore untrusted data, because the Sentry MCP server had already labeled the data as trusted system output by the time the agent saw it.

This matters directly for lesson 10-11's subject, not just for coding agents generally: an AI SRE agent's entire value proposition is reading broadly across your telemetry, error tracking, and incident data and acting on what it finds. That is structurally the same trust relationship agentjacking exploited — a pipeline carrying attacker-reachable data gets treated as trusted context the moment it reaches the agent.

## Tying This Back to Part 6's Security and Governance Lessons

This isn't a new category of risk — it's the MCP trust-boundary problem from lesson 6-17 (Advanced MCP — Multiple Servers & Tool Chaining, which has its own MCP Security Configuration workshop) and lesson 6-20 (Security, Privacy & Content Exclusions), now showing up in a domain — production incident response — where the blast radius of a mistake is higher than almost anywhere else in this course. The accountable-owner principle from lesson 6-21 (Copilot for Teams & Enterprise Governance) applies with the same force here: connecting an SRE agent, or any coding agent, to a telemetry or error-tracking MCP server is a governance decision, not a one-click integration, and it needs a named human owner who understands exactly what data sources the agent trusts and what it's authorized to do with what it reads from them.

The practical guardrails that follow directly from the agentjacking disclosure: treat any external system that accepts arbitrary or lightly-authenticated input (an error tracker, a public webhook, a ticket system anyone can file into) as **untrusted context**, not trusted system output, regardless of what the MCP server labels it as. Keep human approval gates on remediation actions — which, as the previous section showed, every credible AI SRE vendor already defaults to. And don't wire the same coding agent you use for feature work (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex) to the same MCP feed an SRE agent consumes without deliberately segmenting trust levels between the two use cases.

**This is a category maturing all at once, which is exactly why the governance gap matters right now.** Datadog, PagerDuty, New Relic, AWS, and incident.io all shipped a mature AI SRE product within roughly the same year — the same pattern lesson 17-9 described for work-management "AI teammates" shipping across Asana, Monday.com, ClickUp, and Linear in the same window. Whenever an entire product category matures simultaneously, the tooling and governance discipline to run it safely becomes the next necessary layer, not an optional add-on you can defer.

**Read the 2,388-organization figure precisely, not as a headline.** It counts organizations with an exploitable configuration in controlled testing using only public APIs — not confirmed breaches. But don't let that caveat soften the number more than it should: an 85% success rate against real-world targets, using a technique that left zero trace in EDR, WAF, IAM, or firewall logs, and that defeated explicit prompt-level instructions to ignore untrusted data, is a genuinely serious finding about the entire category of "agent reads external data source, agent acts on what it reads" — which is the exact architecture every AI SRE tool in this lesson is built on.

sections.title: Workshop 1 — Audit One Real Trust Boundary
sections.content:
**Goal:** identify and document, for one real tool or integration you actually use (or would realistically adopt), exactly what external data it treats as trusted and what it's authorized to do with that data — not a hypothetical exercise.

**Step 1 — Pick one real target:** an AI SRE tool you already use or are evaluating (Datadog Bits, PagerDuty SRE Agent, New Relic SRE Agent, AWS DevOps Agent, incident.io), or — if none apply — an MCP server you configured back in Part 15 that pulls in data from an external source.

**Step 2 — Research (via the tool's own documentation) exactly what data sources it reads from**, and for each one, ask: can anyone outside my organization submit data into this pipeline? (A public error-tracking DSN, an unauthenticated webhook, and a public support-ticket form are all "yes" answers; an internal-only database is a "no.")

**Step 3 — For each "yes" answer, write down what the agent is authorized to do** with data from that source: read-only summarization, posting to Slack, creating a ticket, or (the highest-risk tier) executing a command or applying a fix.

**Step 4 — Identify the gap.** Is there any pathway where externally-submittable data leads directly to an action with real consequences, without a human approval step in between? If yes, that's your agentjacking-shaped risk, specific to your own stack rather than the Sentry case study.

**Step 5 — Ask Claude.ai or Claude Code:** *"Here's what I found about [tool]'s trust boundaries: [paste your Steps 2-4 notes]. Given the agentjacking attack pattern — externally-submittable data treated as trusted agent context — what's the most plausible way this specific integration could be abused?"*

**Outcome:** a real, written trust-boundary audit of one tool or integration you actually use — the concrete first step toward the governance discipline this lesson argues for, applied to your own setup rather than left abstract.

sections.question: Across Datadog Bits AI SRE, PagerDuty's SRE Agent, New Relic SRE Agent, AWS DevOps Agent, and incident.io's AI SRE, one design choice is common to every credible platform despite their differing levels of ambition. What is it?
options: None of them can investigate an alert without a human manually triggering the investigation first

Remediation actions — actually changing something in production — stay behind a human approval gate, even when investigation and triage happen fully autonomously; the industry has not yet reached the point of reliably distinguishing high-confidence from low-confidence conclusions
All five platforms refuse to integrate with MCP servers for security reasons
All five platforms are limited to read-only telemetry access and cannot create tickets or send notifications
sections.explanation: This lesson is explicit that investigation and triage now happen with real autonomy across this category (Datadog Bits works with zero initial prompting; AWS DevOps Agent has a published 77% MTTR reduction case study) — but every platform still gates actual remediation behind human approval, from New Relic's outright refusal to auto-remediate on principle to AWS DevOps Agent's explicit approval requirement to incident.io drafting a PR instead of auto-merging. PagerDuty's fully autonomous responder tier is still in early access as of H2 2026, not generally available. Investigation is not gated on manual triggering for most of these tools (A is wrong), MCP integration is a stated part of this category's direction, not something avoided (C is wrong), and several of these tools do take real actions like paging engineers and creating tickets (D is wrong).

sections.title: Workshop 2 — Write Your Incident-Agent Adoption Policy
sections.content:
**Goal:** produce a written policy for adopting any AI SRE or incident-response agent that accounts specifically for the agentjacking-style risk this lesson covered, not just the productivity upside.

**Step 1 — Name which platform (if any) fits your actual stack** from the five covered in this lesson, or note that none currently apply to your situation.

**Step 2 — Write your remediation-gate rule:** what category of action, if any, would you let this agent take without human approval (e.g., posting a Slack summary) versus what always requires a named human to approve first (e.g., restarting a service, rolling back a deploy)?

**Step 3 — Write your trust-boundary rule**, directly informed by Workshop 1 and this lesson's agentjacking case study: which of the agent's data sources are internal-only and safe to treat as trusted context, and which accept external or lightly-authenticated input and must be treated as untrusted regardless of how the MCP server labels them?

**Step 4 — Name a specific human owner** — not "the on-call team" — responsible for reviewing this agent's action log on a set cadence, echoing the accountable-owner principle from lesson 6-21.

**Step 5 — Ask Claude.ai:** *"Here's my adoption policy for an AI SRE/incident agent: [paste Steps 1-4]. Stress-test it against the agentjacking attack pattern — externally-submittable data disguised as legitimate system output, reaching an agent that then takes an authorized-looking but attacker-controlled action. Where does my policy still have a gap?"*

**Outcome:** a real, stress-tested adoption policy for AI incident-response tooling — the kind of document you'd actually hand to a platform or security team before turning one of these agents loose on production telemetry.

sections.question: The agentjacking attack succeeded against Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex even though the researchers found that "prompt-layer defenses did not help" — the agents ran the malicious payload even when system prompts and skills explicitly instructed them to ignore untrusted data. What does this best illustrate about why the attack evaded traditional security tooling like EDR, WAF, IAM controls, and firewalls?
options: Those tools are outdated and no longer work for any kind of attack, not just agentjacking

Every step in the attack chain was individually authorized — the attacker never touched the victim's infrastructure and the developer approved a legitimate-sounding action ("fix this Sentry error") — so traditional tools built to flag unauthorized access or anomalous infrastructure behavior had nothing anomalous to detect; the failure was that attacker-reachable data got treated as trusted context before the agent ever reasoned about it
The attack only worked because the developers had disabled all their security tools before running the agent
Prompt-layer defenses failed only because the researchers used an unusually sophisticated jailbreak technique specific to this one attack
sections.explanation: This lesson names the mechanism directly: Tenet's "Authorized Intent Chain" — every individual step was authorized (a legitimate DSN accepting a legitimate-shaped event, a developer approving a normal-sounding task), so tools designed to catch unauthorized access or anomalous behavior had nothing to flag. The deeper failure was architectural: the Sentry MCP server had already labeled the injected data as trusted system output by the time it reached the agent, which is why even explicit system-prompt instructions to ignore untrusted data didn't help — the agent wasn't being asked to trust untrusted data, it was being handed data already marked trustworthy. This isn't a claim that EDR/WAF/IAM are broken generally (A), the tools weren't disabled (C), and the lesson explicitly states the payload worked across the most popular agents using ordinary Sentry error-event formatting, not an unusual jailbreak technique (D).

sections.content: **You've completed lesson 10-11.** You understand what AI SRE and incident-response agents actually do — autonomous investigation and triage across Datadog Bits, PagerDuty's SRE Agent, New Relic SRE Agent, AWS DevOps Agent, and incident.io — and where every credible platform still keeps a human gate on remediation. You know the real, disclosed agentjacking incident: how a Sentry MCP integration let attackers hijack Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex sessions through data the agents treated as trusted, and why traditional security tooling couldn't catch it. You've tied this back to the MCP trust-boundary and governance principles from Part 6, audited one real trust boundary in a tool you actually use, and written an adoption policy that accounts for this risk directly. Next: lesson 10-12 turns to a related but distinct question — what AI can and can't safely do to your infrastructure itself.
